title: Interview | Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi × a16z’s Ben Horowitz: How Enterprise “AI Arms Races” Shape LLM Progress
summary: This dialogue is part of a16z’s AI Revolution series — builders debating where AI stands, where it goes, and which questions remain open. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi and a16z co-founder Ben Horowitz unpack data wars inside and outside the enterprise and how those fights shape LLM
author: Unique Research
html:
Unique Research · Interview / a16z AI Revolution series (CN editorial package) · December 5, 2023 · Speakers: Ali Ghodsi (CEO & co-founder, Databricks) and Ben Horowitz (co-founder, a16z) · CN author: Haoyu

This dialogue is part of a16z’s AI Revolution series — builders debating where AI stands, where it goes, and which questions remain open. Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi and a16z co-founder Ben Horowitz unpack data wars inside and outside the enterprise and how those fights shape LLM development.

Context (CN note): Databricks (2013) was founded by creators of Apache Spark™, Delta Lake, and MLflow. It offers a unified data-intelligence platform for data processing, analytics, and AI apps on a Lakehouse architecture, integrating with existing ETL, ingest, BI, AI, and governance tools. Mission: simplify and democratize data and AI.

Why is enterprise GenAI adoption hard?

Ben: As VCs we see companies with crazy pull — but almost always selling to developers, consumers, or small practices (e.g. law firms). We have not yet seen the same enterprise traction. As enterprise AI infra, why is GenAI hard for big companies?

Ali: Enterprises move slowly — which is wonderful once you crack them, because they rarely eject you. Second, they are terrified about data privacy and security. For 10–20 years everyone talked data as a treasure chest; now they finally believe it and will not hand it over — especially after leak stories and LLMs regurgitating source code. Third: many apps need data that is accurate and error-free.

Ben: Are they right that they need zero-error data?

Ali: Depends on the app. They are cautious and slow — that is large enterprise. And the piece nobody mentions: the internal “chaos war.”

Ben: Who is on the battlefield?

Ali: “I own GenAI, not Ben.” Then everyone says the same. Org fights over ownership — IT vs product vs line of business — and they sandbag each other (“don’t trust Ben’s data handling”). They want GenAI; the road is full of blockers and expense. Whoever cracks that creates an incredible company.

Enterprise data wars

Ben: Firms refuse to give data to OpenAI, Anthropic, Bard, etc. — are they right, or too cautious relative to the value of putting data into a large model?

Ali: They can get value. CEOs who never cared about what we did suddenly want strategy talks: “We have a precious dataset; GenAI looks interesting.” Boards realize GenAI might be the kryptonite that beats a rival — but they insist on building and owning the IP, not handing it to Anthropic or OpenAI. Lines form outside the office claiming they can deliver; leadership is still picking who gets the mandate.

Large LLMs vs small LLMs

Ben: If you hold a huge medical, security, or Nielsen-like dataset, can you beat putting that data into a frontier model by training your own?

Ali: That is why we bought Mosaic. Yes — hard, GPU-hungry. Mosaic’s team found how to do it at scale for others: “Want to train an LLM from scratch? I know the landmines.” They already do this for large customers. Cost and fit depend on dataset and app.

Ben: Good news: it’s my data. But does a bigger general model still win if I drop the same data in — or does a Mosaic-tuned, enterprise-specific model win?

Ali: For a specific app you often do not need a huge model. We can train huge models with Mosaic/Databricks if you have the cash — even a 100-billion-parameter model — but inference then costs more.

Ben: Marginal returns of dataset vs parameter count — diminishing returns on latency and dollars?

Ali: There is a scaling law: grow parameters and you must grow data, or you leave Pareto optimality. Grow either alone and you still improve — at a cost. Enterprise buyers do not ask for a model that answers everything; they ask to spot a manufacturing defect in images. With a good training set a smaller model can beat a giant on accuracy, with lower latency and cost — it just will not moonlight as a physics tutor or weekend entertainment bot.

Ben: Why build a very large model at Databricks at all?

Ali: Follow the scaling law and larger models are more capable — if you can pay, get GPUs, and crack how to fine-tune them. That is today’s research and enterprise holy grail.

Fine-tuning

Ben: Make “fine-tuning” concrete.

Ali: Take a strong foundation model and lightly adapt it to shine on other tasks. Many techniques exist; nobody has fully cracked adapting without touching the whole model — expensive at serve time. If you ship a thousand specialized versions each loaded on GPUs, serving explodes. The grail is one smart brain plus small task modules (prefix tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, etc.). No decisive winner yet. Ideal end-state: one giant intelligent base model plus specialized add-ons for defect detection or translation — compute- and energy-efficient. Nobody has truly shipped that yet. Meanwhile many customers want cheaper, smaller, accurate specialists. After Mosaic we did not even unleash sales — demand outstrips GPU supply; we cannot sell it to every customer who wants “a thousand things.”

Ben: How fragmented will apps become vs one AWS/GCP/Azure-like brain once fine-tuning works?

Ali: Closer to the latter with lots of specialization on shared foundations — not training from scratch every time. The industry may be over-indexing like 2000 Cisco: best router = own the internet forever; peak ~$5T narrative, valued above Microsoft. Same story now: biggest LLM owns AI and humanity’s future. Like the internet, Uber-like apps appear later. Marc’s “Why AI Will Save the World” points the same way — not one OpenAI/Databricks/Anthropic model for every use case. A doctor you trust to heal you takes much more. Cisco routers and LLMs both matter; Cisco is still valuable — focus is just a bit overheated.

Open-source AI

Ben: Big model vendors say stop open source. Fair grievance? How does Databricks see Mosaic and LLaMA?

Ali: If original LLaMA never shipped, AI would be far behind. Scale plus openness changed everything. Weights leak; people keep adapting; distillation pulls behavior into smaller weights. Scarcity of GPUs pushes efficient tricks (fast transformers). A truly great giant model usually has little incentive to release. Open source usually lags proprietary — except rare Linux-like flips. Hard to predict; today you need huge GPU pools. When GPUs abound or training becomes far more sample-efficient, universities — currently locked out of the game — will race to crack cheaper release paths. Open vs proprietary competition continues; returns diminish as we hit scaling walls. Moving right on the X-axis eventually yields AGI — but with diminishing returns.

“Benchmarks are nonsense”

Ben: Will we stall before AGI and need real breakthroughs beyond scale?

Ali: In almost every serious use case (medicine, law) you still need a human in the loop. Models are dumb and err.

Ben: But they beat doctors on medical exams.

Ali: Funny thing — I think all LLM benchmarks are nonsense. Imagine giving students the exam and answers the night before. MMLU is web multiple choice; you can train on it deliberately or accidentally contaminate. They memorize. Transfer from exam memory to real diagnosis is unproven. Everyone games benchmarks. I would love a sealed doctor-designed benchmark you never see — submit the model, get a score. Until then: human-in-the-loop; we need a phase-change improvement before humans leave most important tasks.

Why Ali is not terrified of today’s AI

Ben: Morality of large vs open models — threat size?

Ali: I do not have all answers. Job-loss class: we have automated for 300 years; highest-GDP countries automate most and still have high employment. Stopping progress is dumb; economics is efficiency. Malicious human misuse has existed since hammers. The big open question Marc ducks: a superintelligence that decides to destroy us?

Ben: “Decide” confuses me — free will is not how these machines work. No LLM has ever decided anything.

Ali: If something this smart also controls actuators without guardrails, damage can be large. I am less worried near-term because: (1) training a new frontier model is extremely expensive/hard — asymmetry vs just querying it; if training a SOTA model took 10 minutes, bad actors would AutogPT a million variants and race. A better transformer that turns 10 minutes into 2 minutes starts a self-improving loop. Today that asymmetry is our lifeline. (2) Machines cannot yet biologically self-reproduce / auto-fab new machines. Crack that loop and we are in trouble — we are far from it. Just sliding scaling laws does not solve those two problems.

Ben: On that cheerful note — thanks Ali, thanks everyone.

1 CN image; attach on ingest. CN author: Haoyu; review: Qiuping.

— END —
